en: The *Kālacakrāvatāra* by the scholar Abhayākaragupta. Oṃ, homage to Mañjuśrī!

I pay homage to my own innate, all-encompassing, and universal body of the Victor (Jina), which possesses a form that is both formless and composed of form and so forth; which bears a body of manifold appearances, yet is of an undifferentiated nature and the boundless bliss of non-dual wisdom and compassion.
Those luminaries which bestow beauty upon the sky and announce both prosperity and calamity,
shining as if within the heart of the Tathāgata, now triumph over the darkness.

For here, because the heterodox teachers (tīrthika), afflicted by avarice, have concealed the established astronomical system (siddhānta) and composed a simplified calculation (laghukaraṇa) with many complications such that it is no longer understood even now, that [system] is here set forth.
One should write four hundred and three [years].
When the year begins from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, then it must be combined with this [correction].

That [number], diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, becomes the pure annual constant (*varṣadhruvaka*). That, multiplied by twelve (*arkka*), is the lunar-month aggregate (*māsapiṇḍa*) starting from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon (*amāvāsya*).
When the [lunar] month beginning with Caitra occurs,

that [remainder] is placed in two positions; the lower one is multiplied by four, divided by zero-three-one (130), and when the remainder of the division is discarded and the quotient is added to the upper position,
the pure sum of months is obtained at the top.

But when she is two years old, then a year should be calculated as consisting of thirteen months; one month [of the current year] should be counted, and the entry into the month of Caitra should not be made. Having placed that aggregate of pure months in three places, it is multiplied by eleven (kara-śikhin) in the middle place; from the lower place, the quotient obtained by dividing by six (ṣaḍ-bhāga) is to be subtracted.
If there should be a remainder from the division, then the quotient obtained from dividing by six must also be subtracted.
Here, the quotient obtained from dividing by sixty the number thirty added to the lower [value] should be added to the upper [value] increased by two.
The remainder of the division shall be the *daṇḍapiṇḍa*.
The remainder of seven divisions at the top shall be the *vārapiṇḍa*. Nothing is obtained [in the quotient].

Again, having placed the pure accumulated months mixed with one hundred and twelve in two places, the remainder from the division by six in the lower position shall be the component of the total. The quotient obtained from the division, increased by five and multiplied by two, should be added to the upper position.
Then, the remainder from dividing the upper position by twenty-eight shall be the *pada*-total.

From the *atravāra-piṇḍa*, the sequence of *daṇḍa*, *pada*, *piṇḍa*, and *piṇḍāvayava* should be written down one below the other. Then, the pure months situated in the three positions, multiplied by the lords of the middle places, are divided below by forty-nine; the quotient obtained is added to two, and the result is divided by sixty *ghaṭīs*. The remainder of the division is to be known as the *nakṣatra-ghaṭīs*, while the quotient, doubled, is placed at the top.
Then, the remainder after dividing the head [of the calculation] by twenty-seven should be known as the aggregate of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-piṇḍa*).

Here, below the aggregate of the *ṛtu* [periods], the aggregate of the *ṛtu*-ghaṭīs should be written. When neither the year is entered into the annual zodiacal sign (*varṣa-rāśi*) nor the month into the monthly aggregate (*māsa-piṇḍa*), [the following applies].

Then, month by month, one, thirty-two, and two—one each—should be added respectively to the components of the weekday, the *daṇḍas*, the *padas*, and the *piṇḍas*. Furthermore, two *ghaṭīs* and eleven should be added.
At the commencement of a new year, a different set of weekdays, *piṇḍas*, and so forth must be calculated.
This [calculation] is for the purpose of determining the weekday for every day.

For the purpose of calculating the lunar day (*tithi*), the elapsed and current lunar days of the present month, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), are to be added or subtracted, or added again, respectively, to the weekdays, *nāḍīs*, and *padas*.
When two [units] are obtained as the fourteenth part of the *piṇḍa*, the *piṇḍa* is even;
when one or three are obtained, it is odd. It should be added [to the weekday].
There is no further portion beyond this,
because no more *piṇḍas* are obtained above twenty-seven;
[this is] by dividing by twenty-eight.

Therefore, when added to the thirty lunar days (*tithis*), they do not exceed fifty-seven. When the remainder of the division is even, lunar steps (*candrapadas*) are to be added; when odd, they are to be subtracted. In the case of zero, zero is purified. In the case of three, ten, and one lunar step, [the results are] twenty; in the case of five, two, and twelve, [they are] ten; in the case of eleven and three, [they are] twenty minus one.

In the twenty-second [day], in the five apertures, there are twenty-four Victors (Jinas); in the seventh, twenty-five. In that [seventh], all the solar [units] manifested through the divisions of the sun are to be added or subtracted.
"Purified" means that nothing at all is to be added or subtracted.
"In that" refers to the aggregate of *ghaṭīs*.
The solar positions are determined by the division by twelve (*arkaprabheda*).

In that process, there is a subtraction of twelve from the sun, and when there is a subtraction of twelve, it is a debt; when there is an addition of twelve, it is a credit—this is the solar division (*sūryaprabheda*).

This is what is meant: having either added or subtracted the quotient obtained from the division by five (*bhūta*) and so forth according to the method to be described, the days of the week and the traversed positions are combined; this total is called "Ravi" (the Sun) if it falls within the solar course.
It is to be added.
Then it is to be added to the ghatis of the weekday.
Furthermore, it is to be added to the solar longitude and subtracted from the lunar longitude.

The two [groups] of the Moon are the pure Sun and the Moon-Sun; these are the lunar positions among the elements (bhūta). Among the elements, there are four (vedas), three (śikhi), two (kara), and one (śaśin) in the eastern part and likewise in the western part.

In the eastern part, having drawn a horizontal line in the middle according to the upward sequence of the moon, one should write them in the western part below, following the downward sequence of the moon; thus there are fourteen.
In this way, all the omissions consist of ghaṭikās.
In this case, the remainder from the fourteen-fold division indicates the position of the movement; that which is above it is the actual movement.
A planet has entered therein.
Having multiplied the components of the aggregate by that [remainder], one takes the quotient obtained through division by one hundred and twenty-six.
In the first half [of the verse], the "eaten" (bhukta) step is mentioned;
in the second half, having abandoned that, the "uneaten" (abhukta) step itself is to be added to or subtracted from the place of the *vāra*-ghaṭikās.

This is what is said: having mixed the result obtained by division by the elapsed [periods] and so forth according to the method to be described, and having subtracted it, however many combined solar steps there may be, that is called the "sun" (*ravi*); if [this] is in the solar longitude...
It should be added;
then it should be added to the weekday-count.
Alternatively, it should be subtracted from the solar longitude.
Then, regarding this [diagram], that which is to be abandoned is as follows:

there are two types of lunar positions—the pure solar and the lunar-solar. Among the elements (bhūta) and non-elements (abhūta), the Vedas (4), fire (3), rays (12), and moon (1) are in the eastern part and the western part.

In the eastern part, having drawn a vertical line in sequence from above and a horizontal line in the middle, one should write the states starting with the moon (śaśi) and so forth in reverse order in the western part; thus, there are fourteen.
Thus, all [the movements] consist of *ghaṭikās* of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Here, the true movement (*saccārapada*) established by the remainder of the fourteenth part is the true movement above that;
there, the planet has entered.
Having multiplied that by the divisor, one obtains the quotient with a remainder of one hundred and twenty-six.
In the first half [of the month], this is the elapsed *pada*;
however, in the second half, having subtracted that, the unelapsed *pada* itself is to be added to or subtracted from the positions of the weekday and *ghaṭikās*.
Since the *ravikās* in this world are impure, for the sake of obtaining pure *ravikās*,
one establishes the days of the week, starting with one and so forth, beginning from Sunday (*āditya-vāra*) and the rest.
On the lunar day (*tithi*), the *daṇḍas* and so forth must be consumed starting from sunrise.

For the purpose of determining the Sun’s daily transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), the lunar day (*tithi*) stated as beginning with the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) is placed in two locations. In one place, it is multiplied by four *daṇḍas*.

In the other, it is multiplied by twenty or twenty-two *pāṇīpala*s according to the method of the *Karaṇas*, or by twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s according to the arrangement of the *Siddhāntas*. Having divided [the result] by sixty, the quotient is added to the upper [value]. Then, having divided the upper *daṇḍas* by sixty, the quotient is applied to the asterism; the remainder of the division is the *daṇḍas* of the asterism.
One should add [the degrees]. Furthermore, one should write the *pāṇīpala* below the *daṇḍa* of the asterism (*nakṣatra*).

When the asterism, its *daṇḍa*, the total sum (*piṇḍa*), and the *pāṇīpala* have been placed in two positions, in one of them—[the first]—for the sake of the Sun, those six asterisms in three quarters (*tripada*) are to be subtracted.
The sign that remains after subtracting Aries, Aśvinī, and so forth, shall be the next birth-sign.
As it is said:
"In Aries, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and Libra, [the lords] are the Moon, Venus, and the Sun."
Mars, the minister (Saturn), Rāhu, Mercury, Saturn, and Venus [are situated] in Sagittarius, from the beginning to the end of Scorpio.
Regarding the phrase "beginning and end":
Saturn is at the beginning of the bow (Cāpa) and Ketu is at its end.

Here, if the debt (*ṛṇa*) is greater than the [remaining] portion of the zodiacal sign, then it should be subtracted after adding twenty-seven to the position of the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) in the circle of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
If the remainder after subtraction is equal to half the circle (180°),
then that half-circle must be subtracted;
at that very point, the inverse sine (cotjyā) is to be understood.
If the half-circle has not been subtracted, the process is exactly the same.

From the asterism divided by sixty, add the minutes situated below; then, having determined the zodiacal sign-quarter (rāśicaraṇa) by discarding the quotient obtained from dividing by fifteen (bhūtavahnicandra), one should know that in the slow-motion calculation (mandakārya), there are six sign-quarters for the signs beginning with Scorpio (karka) and the others, which are five [in number] starting from the birth-sign.

There are exactly this many *pada*s for the slow motion (*mandakārya*) of all planets; when the quotient is obtained by means of the *bhūta* (five) and other values, it should be understood that the planet stands in the first *pada* in every case.
Then, the operation to be performed as will be described later—beginning with "divided by that"—should be carried out.
In that case, for the slow motion of all planets, [the result] should be known as a debt (*ṛṇa*) in direct order (*krama*) and a credit (*dhana*) in reverse order (*utkrama*).
Then, from the portion already traversed, a second portion to be traversed is taken.

From the remaining *nāḍīs* divided by that [portion], the portions to be traversed—along with the portions already traversed by the element-division (*bhūtādi-bhāga*)—are combined with the *caraṇas* (quarters) traversed by the planet according to the sign (*rāśi*) in the first half [of the circle].

However, in the latter half, having subtracted the portion to be traversed obtained by division, the untraversed *caraṇa*-steps are combined with the other portion to be traversed; these are to be added to or subtracted from the planetary motion according to whether they constitute a debt or an asset.
This very channel is the pure solar *ravikā* of the Sun;
in the place of the asterism of the Sun, the asterism and so forth have been consumed,
and what remains of that which was consumed is yet to be consumed.
This applies even when the moon and the yoga to be described are present.

Now, the impure solar values (*aśuddharavikāḥ*) of the sun are stated: for the sun, they are time (1), taste (6), serpent (8), ten (10), day-maker (12), Rudra (11), direction (10), serpent (8), and six (6).

At the end of the northern course, fire (3) and ether (0) become wealth and debt respectively in the north and south; thus the Sun moves for six months through divisions of fortnights due to the distinction of monthly transits (*saṅkrānti*).
Here, in Cancer and so forth, there is a wound (*vraṇa*) in one fortnight and time (*kāla*) [in the other];
in the second [fortnight] of Cancer, there is taste (*rasa*).

In this manner, up until the bow [sign], there is fire; at the end of the northern course, there is space; and likewise, from Capricorn onwards, there is wealth. For the purpose of calculating the Moon’s transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the lunar days (*tithi*) stated for the white fortnight and so forth should be added to the solar transit in the place of the lunar mansions.

Subsequently, those lunar days, multiplied by six (*rasa*) and placed in another location, combined with the minutes and so forth of the transit of the weekday, constitute the negative minutes (*ṛṇaghaṭī*) of the Sun.
In the place of the ghatis, it should be understood as a debt;
from this, the lunar motion (candrabhoga) shall be obtained.
The lunar motion is derived from the solar motion (sūryabhoga).
The lunar days (tithis) of the bright fortnight and so forth, when doubled and diminished by one, shall—provided it is possible—be the *karaṇa* [name] when reduced by a remainder of seven.
The *karaṇa* is the duration; that is, the duration of the lunar day itself.
Herein lies the general rule.
In the place of the breath, those breaths which do not remain above enter into the *pāṇīpala*s as divided by a sixth part;
those too remain for half of sixty [moments].
The quotient obtained by dividing by sixty enters into the *ghaṭīs*;
likewise, the *ghaṭīs* also enter into the weekday or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). The weekdays, having reached seven, likewise perish.
Do not even the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) here exist as such?
Likewise, the yogas are also thus: one mansion consists of sixty *daṇḍas*; [the triad of] the day of the week (*vāra*), the yoga, and the day (*dina*).
In that context, the *vāras* (days of the week) are seven, beginning with Āditya; the *tithis* (lunar days) are fifteen, beginning with the first day (*pratipad*);

and the *nakṣatras* (lunar mansions) are: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā.
The twenty-seven [asterisms] are: Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Raivatī.
Likewise, the [twenty-seven] yogas are:
Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, and Vyatīpāta.
The twenty-seven *karaṇas* are: Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti;
the seven [movable] *karaṇas* are: Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi;
and the eleven [fixed] *karaṇas* are: Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna.

In that regard, beginning from the latter half of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), each [deity] possesses [the day] for four watches (*prahara*) respectively; this sequence is repeated again and again until the first half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī*), at which point the possession of the seven [deities] is complete.
From the latter half of that same day until the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight, the possession of the other four [deities] occurs.

Having divided the duration of the lunar day (tithi-bhoga) into two equal parts, one should understand the distinction between the first half and the second half. This is the sequence of the fivefold calendar (pañcāṅga), consisting of the day of the week, the lunar day, the asterism (nakṣatra), the yoga, and the karaṇa.
Aries consists of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and one quarter of Kṛttikā.

In this manner, by means of nine quarters each, the twelve zodiac signs—Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—are to be understood as corresponding to the months beginning with Vaiśākha.
[The lords of the signs are] Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, [Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun].
Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn are esteemed as the lords of the Kṣatriya; their positions in these signs follow this sequence.

The pure years (*śuddhavarṣāṇi*)—that is, the pure years (*śuddhābdāḥ*) increased by eight—are multiplied by four hundred. These are then diminished by the pure years increased by eight, separately. The resulting quotient, increased by two, becomes the days of the week (*vārāḥ*).

From the remainders of the division, having multiplied by sixty and converted into *nāḍīs*, the quotient obtained by dividing by seven and so forth is to be taken; the remainder of the division is to be discarded.
To the obtained ghaṭīs, thirty are added; the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty is added to two, and this enters into the weekday.
The remainder of the division is the weekday-ghaṭī constant (vāraghaṭikā-dhruvaka) below.
Furthermore, the remainder from dividing the weekdays by seven shall be the weekday constant for the solar ingress (saṃkrānti) at the top.

In this context, when the sun leaves Pisces and enters Aries, they are "projected" (kṣipyante), thus they are called "projectors" (kṣepakāḥ); these are twelve [degrees] in Aries and the following signs in due order:
[the values are] 1, 7, 15, 4, 3, 5, 1, 5, 1, 1, 7, and 1 in the third [sign].
The moon is the foremost among the Vedas; the eyes and hands together are two; and the eyes of knowledge are sixty in the sixth [house].
Six, two moons; five, one moon; seven, two, fire; six, moon, four, mountains, worlds;
six, Vedas; zero, zero; and two, five, a quarter—these are the values for the Sun in the sign of Pisces.
This is their placement (*nyāsa*).

Among these, for each of the twelve compartments, the first [value] is to be placed in the weekday-constant (*vāradhruva*), and the second is the *ghaṭī*-constant beginning with fifty-seven; thus, the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) and its duration in days and *ghaṭīs* are to be known from this *karaṇa*.
Now, the calculation of days (*ahan-gaṇa*) is stated for the purpose of determining the duration of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-bhoga*) starting from Mars (*maṅgala*).

The pure months, multiplied by thirty for the purpose of obtaining the heap of days, are added to the lunar dates (tithis) stated for the bright fortnight and so forth; having placed them in two positions, one should add the quotient obtained by dividing the lower heap by 703 to the middle heap. Then, the upper heap diminished by the quotient obtained from dividing the middle heap by 64 shall be the uncorrected day-count (asphuṭadinagaṇa). Having placed that in two positions, one should divide one of them by seven for the sake of the days of the week.
If that day were not the [correct] weekday,
then one or more units should be added to or subtracted from the first term so that the weekday may coincide;
thereafter, the sphuṭa (corrected) ahargaṇa is obtained.

For the sake of determining the auspicious [longitude] of Mars, one should add 167 to the clear count of days; from this, the quotient obtained by division by the days of Mars’s revolution—namely, 240—is to be subtracted as a completed cycle of signs (*rāśiparivarta*). The same applies to the other planets. The remainder is multiplied by the [number of] lunar mansions (27) and divided by the days of its own revolution; the quotient is the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) above. From that remainder, multiplied by sixty and divided by the days of its own revolution, the quotient is the *ghaṭīs* below; the *pāṇīpala*s and so forth are as before. This result, beginning with the lunar mansion, is placed in two positions; in one place, nine and a half lunar mansions are added.
These are to be subtracted.
Then, for the Sun, the sum of Aries and Āśvinī is to be known as stated.
For one situated in Viśeṣa, eighteen *tattvas* are the *padas* in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakārya*).
In the subsequent [calculation], such as that involving the asterisms and so forth, [the values] are either to be added or subtracted.
Thus concludes the purification of Mars in slow motion (*mandakarma*).
However, in fast motion (*śīghrakarma*), one should place the already purified slow-motion value of Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn in two places.

One [unit] is subtracted from the solar longitude when it is devoid of *ravikā*; this is not subtracted when the lunar day (*tithi*) has been mixed. In the procedure for discarding six constellations (*ṣaḍnakṣatra*), one should subtract three-quarters [of a unit].
Thereafter, the sequence beginning with "if the solar [longitude] is a debt" and ending with "thus is the order" should be understood.
Here, in the calculation of the swifter [motion], wealth (*dhana*) is to be added in direct order (*krama*), and debt (*ṛṇa*) is to be subtracted in reverse order (*utkrama*).

The purification of that [remainder] should be performed as follows: having determined the quotient obtained from the divisor that establishes the planetary *caraṇas* (steps), the remainder is to be subtracted.

By multiplying that very remainder by sixty and dividing by the divisor, one obtains a portion of that step (*tatpadāṃśa*). In the first half [of the zodiac], the *caraṇas* traversed by the planet are accumulated according to the sign and *caraṇa* divisions, together with that portion of the step.
In the second half, however, having discarded the portion of the step obtained from the division, the *caraṇas* not yet traversed are calculated together with the other portion of the step.
In another place, for slow-moving planets, these values are to be added to or subtracted from the pure planetary longitude.

Here, there are fourteen squares; the Jina (24) is threefold; the eyes (2), the moon (1), the hands (2), twice eight (16), and the days (7); from the root of Śiva (11) and Vahni (3); Rudra (11), eight (8), and Vahni (3); below the sky (0), arms (2), and serpents (8);

three, fivefold, those [are] for the earth (1) of the auspicious one from the root. Thus, from the horizontal line: the directions (10), directions (10), the navel (9), Vasu (8), six, six, two, one, the root (1), the limbs (5), and the chest (6).
The *randhra* (nine), *rūdra* (eleven), and *nṛyoga* (thirty-three) are the steps of the Guru for swift calculation.

From the root [of the sum]—six seasons, five arrows, five arrows, four Vedas, four Vedas, two eyes, and two eyes, and zero—the steps of Śauri (Saturn) are two, four, five arrows (five), eight, and three.
This is half a verse.
Likewise, having placed the slow sun (mandasūrya) in two places, one should subtract it from both the motion of Mercury and the motion of Venus.
Then,
following the procedure beginning with "of that subtraction" and ending with "unmoved degrees" as previously stated for Mars, those [results] are to be added to or subtracted from the other slow sun.
In this very manner, the periods (bhoga) of Mercury and Venus occur.
From the [period] of the Lord of the Earth (Mars), there are the lunar days (tithi); from that, the scents (six), the limbs (six), and the auspicious mountains (seven).
The fifth is from the Mūla [nakṣatra], and then twenty and twenty-eight.
Thirty-four for Saumya; twice for Strī and Suta;
twice for Jana; twice for Akṣi; Doṣa is fifteen; from Mūla, eight; and likewise six, ten, and eleven.

The [mean] anomaly, the [mean] anomaly of the apsis, the [mean] anomaly of the node, and so forth, as well as the position for the fast motion of Venus—thus concludes the purification of the fast-motion equations for Mars and the other planets.

For the slow-motion equation, in order to purify Mercury, one should take the true number of elapsed days, multiply by one hundred, subtract three thousand two hundred and seven, and divide by the days of Mercury’s revolution (one hundred and twenty-seven thousand, six hundred and ten); the result obtained, and so forth, is in *pāṇīpala* and so on.
The section ending with "iti" should be treated as an auspicious procedure. This movement of the asterisms and so forth is stated for the purpose of the *śīghrakarma* (quick calculation).
Therefore, for that purpose, having placed the solar longitude in two locations and subtracted the sun from one of them, sixteen and a half asterisms are to be subtracted from the solar longitude.

Then, having performed the operations beginning with Aries and ending with the addition or subtraction according to the sun's position as previously stated, those [asterisms] are to be added to or subtracted from the other solar longitude.
Thus, Mercury is pure in its slow motion.
This other solar revolution, having attained the nature of pure Mercury through its slow motion (*mandakarma*), is called the "slow Sun" for the purpose of the fast motion (*śīghrakarma*).
In the calculation of the slow motion, there are one hundred and seventy-three steps (*pada*).

For the purpose of purifying Jupiter, one should proceed as with Mars, starting from the calculation of the clear day-count (*sphuṭāhargana*) reduced by 2060, and then taking the quotient obtained by dividing by 4314, and so forth.
Here, however, there is this distinction: the twelve asterisms (*nakṣatra*) to be subtracted are the steps consisting of 918.

For the purpose of purifying Venus, one should perform everything as with Mercury, starting from the clear day-count multiplied by ten and reduced by 84, and then taking the quotient obtained by dividing by 2527, and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: six nakṣatras are to be subtracted, and the pādas are fifty-two and one (521).

For the sake of purifying Saturn, from the count of true days diminished by eighty-four thousand four hundred and eighty (84,480), the quotient obtained by division by sixty-six, seven, zero, and one (66701), and so forth, should be performed as for Mars.
The distinction, however, is that eighteen nakṣatras are to be subtracted, and the pādas are twenty-two and fifteen (2215).
Thus ends the purification of Mercury and the other planets in their slow-motion (manda-karman).

Furthermore, when the planetary longitude is purified by the slow-motion and then purified by the fast-motion (śīghra-karman), the planetary longitude becomes truly purified by both motions. Scholars of the scriptures do not hold that the planetary longitude purified by the slow-motion is one thing and the planetary longitude purified by the fast-motion is another; they maintain that these are not distinct.

There is purified enjoyment through two types of action: for the Sun, by slow action alone; for the Moon, by swift action alone; and for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, by both. For the purpose of calculating Rāhu’s transit through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), one should subtract from the pure months—increased by two and twelve—the degrees [required] for a half-month (*pakṣa*). For the full moon, to calculate the lunar eclipse, subtract from those increased by one half-month; for the new moon, to calculate the solar eclipse, subtract from those increased by two half-months. From the resulting *pakṣa-maṇḍalas* of Rāhu, the quotient obtained by dividing by the degrees of sky, seasons, and oceans (460) must be discarded.
From the remaining degrees, for the purpose of determining the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*), multiply by twenty-seven; the result divided by ten gives the lunar mansion.
From the remainder, multiply by sixty; the result divided by ten gives the *ghaṭīs*.
From that remainder as well, in the same manner, [multiply by sixty and divide by ten] to obtain the *liptās*.
The remainder of that, divided by six and multiplied by ten, yields the breaths (*śvāsa*).
By subtracting this obtained value—expressed in asterisms (*nakṣatra*) and so forth—from twenty-seven asterisms, the "mouth-enjoyment" (*mukhabhoga*) of Rāhu is determined.
That same mouth-enjoyment, when added to thirteen and a half asterisms, becomes the "tail-enjoyment" (*pucchabhoga*).
Thereafter, in the solar transit for each month, there are two constellations and eleven ghaṭikās; over six months, this amounts to twelve constellations and sixty-six ghaṭikās.
Thus, thirteen constellations and fifty-three [ghaṭikās] arise.
Here, in the solar transit—that is, during a solar eclipse or the transit of the new moon—the *ravikā* (correction for the sun's motion) is to be added or subtracted.
Then, having subtracted forty-five *ghaṭikās* from Rāhu’s orbital period (*bhoga*), one should subtract the remainder as the lunar mansion’s orbital period (*nakṣatrabhoga*).
In that case, if the lunar mansion is equal [in duration] to either the mouth or the tail of Rāhu, then an eclipse occurs, and not otherwise.
Alternatively, having calculated the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) by the previously mentioned method, one should subtract the solar orbital period from Rāhu’s mouth-orbital period or tail-orbital period.
During a lunar eclipse on the full moon day, one should subtract the Moon's longitude from the longitude of Rāhu’s mouth or from the longitude of Rāhu’s tail.
An eclipse occurs when [the Moon] is at the same degree of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) as either the mouth or the tail;
not otherwise.

For here, at the junction of the lunar nodes (*parvasandhi*)—either at the end of the new moon or the end of the full moon—the orbs of the sun and the moon enter the orb of Rāhu. The term "orb" (*maṇḍala*) refers to sixty *nāḍikās*, which is the duration of the transit through one asterism (*nakṣatra*). This should be understood as consisting of twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and sixteen digits (*kalā*). In that regard, if the transit of these two is cleared within the transit of Rāhu, then there is a total eclipse lasting for the full sixty *nāḍikās*.
When half the [lunar] portion is purified, there is a half-bite (*ardhagrāsa*).
As long as the fourth part of the digit (*kalā*), which consists of four *nāḍīs*, has entered Rāhu’s orbit, the conjunction of the planets is to be known.
And when Rāhu swallows it during the [portion of the] face, then it is the eastern part.
And the rear portion [is assigned] to the tail and the coils;
in this manner, the distribution of the other directions is to be understood as the turning [of the serpent]. This is the interpretation of the commentary, and it occurs precisely within six months.
In ultimate reality, Rāhu, whose nature is darkness, swallows the moon itself because of its cool rays.
It is not the sun;
rather, at the time of the end of the new moon, because the moon has entered the sun,
there is the conventional expression that "the sun swallows [the moon]."

Thus ends the purification of Rāhu. Ketu, having entered the solar disc, moves for four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *liptās* every day; its motion through the sun is [calculated as] two and a half *liptās* more than that of the sun. In its direct motion (*śīghracāra*), it moves forward in regular order, and in its retrograde motion (*vakracāra*), it moves backward in reverse order.
Having remained thus for three years, it emerges;
and having emerged, two *ghaṭīs* arise every day,
and that *ghaṭī* is one-quarter [of a day].

For one month, Ketu, consisting of fifty-six *liptās*, is seen like a star without smoke; thereafter, for one fortnight, it appears as a smoky comet (*dhūmaketu*). Thus, at the end of one and a half months, it becomes invisible again within the solar disc in the same manner for three years.
Its first rising is to be known by observing its established [period];
likewise, its rising once is understood to last for an infinite time—this is the purification of Ketu.
Herein lies this general rule.

In the case of a swift motion (*śīghrakarman*), when a planet has risen from the solar disc and moves forward, its longitude (*bhoga*) in the first half of the fourteen *carana*-units and a half is said to be in swift motion (*śīghracāra*);
in the second half, the motion is slow (*mandacāra*).
Thereafter, when half a circle has been traversed, there is a retrogression of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatrotkrama*).
In the first half [of the circle], there is clockwise rotation (cakracāra), while in the second half,
it is called outward movement (nirgamagati) due to the relinquishing of the zodiacal signs and lunar mansions (rāśinakṣatra).
In this sequence, in the first half, there is an increase in wealth and the planets face the east.
In the latter half [of the year], there is loss of wealth for those facing south;
in the former half, during the upward progression, there is an increase in debt for those facing west;
and in the latter half, there is a reduction of debt for those facing north.

The orientation of these [planets] toward other directions occurs due to portents (*ariṣṭa*) and the like; however, by their very nature, Rāhu moves clockwise around Mount Meru facing westward, while the other planets face eastward.
Consequently, because they are obscured by the rays of the sun, the sun appears to set; it is not that the planet is entirely non-existent.

Furthermore, in this same manner, here in this region, due to the increase and decrease in the movement of the sun and moon, there is an increase in the day by the number of *nāḍīs* obtained as a tenth part of the sixty *nāḍīs* that constitute a day-and-night (*ahorātra*).

At night there is a decrease. From the boundary of the Dakṣiṇāgni circle up to the boundary of the Mahāhimavat circle, for six months during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), [the day increases] by seventy-five thousand *yojanas*. Likewise, from the boundary of the Mahāhimavat circle up to the boundary of the Dakṣiṇāgni circle, for six months during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), there is an increase at night and a decrease in the day.
This being so, it should be understood that every day and night there is a decrease or increase of two *liptās*.

Likewise, from the lands of Bhota, Līca, China, and so forth, up to the region of Sambhala, there is a decrease or increase of three *liptās* plus four breaths (*śvāsa*) every day and night; in the Kailāśa region, this is by six parts; and further north from the Kailāśa region, as far as the Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*), there is a decrease or increase of three *liptās* plus four breaths every day and night.

Outside the Himālaya, in the eight directions, there is a single sphere of the lunar mansions and zodiac signs in the form of a circle. In its center is the equatorial line (*viṣuva-rekhā*). On both sides of this very line, the stars revolve in the shape of a bow; here, in the middle of the sky, the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī revolve like a bullock carrying a load on its head until they reach the midpoint of Citrā in the northern direction of the line.

On the south side, however, starting from the middle of Citrā and ending with Revatī, likewise two and a quarter lunar mansions constitute one zodiac sign (*rāśi*). In this way, there are twelve signs, and the planets are their consumers.
Furthermore, on the northern edge of this sphere, it proceeds from the northern fire-circle (*vahnivalaya*) onwards.
The southern extremity, however, touches the southern limit of the Himavat mountain during the northern course;
during the southern course,
it moves from the southern extremity toward the southern circle of fire and so forth.
The northern limit of the cold ocean touches the northern edge [of Jambudvīpa].

And these constellations and so forth revolve around Sumeru by the power of their motion, forming a spherical shape. The measurement of this sphere extends from the Southern Fire-enclosure (*dakṣiṇāgni-valaya*) to the Mahāhimavat mountains, being three hundred and fifty [yojanas].
[The sun traverses] thousands of *yojanas*.
From these [total distances], the sun relinquishes daily a directional portion obtained by dividing by one hundred and eighty-two and a half, which represents half a day for each mandala.
Thus, the transverse movement of the sun across the twelve sectors (*khaṇḍa*) is to be understood; this is the path of calculation (*karaṇamārga*).
However, even by this method of calculation, there is never absolute purity for the Sun;
when the Sun’s longitude is thus impure, Mars and the other planets, though corrected,
do not become true [sphuṭa], like trees whose roots have perished.

Therefore, the established method is stated as follows: On level ground, having fixed a gnomon twelve *vitastis* in length at the center of a circle measuring one cubit in diameter, when the shadow of the gnomon in the forenoon gradually contracts from the outside and enters the central point of the line on the circumference of the circle,
then the mark made at that spot— known as the "crow's foot"— is the western direction.
"In the afternoon, however, spreading out gradually from the center of the mandala," and so forth.

One should mark the previous point; that very [point] is the east and so on. Here, holding a thread over one mark, one should draw the mandala line toward the west using a small stick from another mark. And holding a thread over the other mark, one should do the same.
It should be in the shape of a fish.
Between those two circles, the middle of the fish's mouth faces south and the middle of its tail faces north;

thus, the cardinal directions are determined. Having erased those two circles at that spot, the examination should be performed at midday, beginning from the tenth day prior to the first day of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).
There, on the first day, the northern limit-line of the mandala enters the center of the mandala from its middle;
that day is the day of the sun’s northern solstice transition (uttarāyaṇa-saṃkrānti).
By that weekday, by that lunar day, by that yoga, and by that karaṇa;
on that day, the solar longitude begins with Vaiśākha and so forth.
By nine months, there are twenty [degrees] in the place of the asterism for the nine signs beginning with Aries.
Fifteen *ghaṭikās* at the place of the *ghaṭikā* is the root constant (*mūla-dhrūvaka*).
To that constant, one should add four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *pāṇīpalas* every day,
and then subtract the solar signs (*ravikā-pādāni*) according to the previously stated method beginning with "the six constellations plus three quarters are to be subtracted," and so forth.
And so it is said in the *Mūlatantra*: "Starting from the [beginning of the] solstice, [the correction] should be applied every day until another solstice occurs;
by means of the performance of the prescribed rites, the position of the sun is to be purified."

Thus, the results regarding the days of the week, lunar dates, asterisms, yogas, karaṇas, zodiac signs, fields, transits, and planets are easily understood from other sources and are not elaborated upon here. Having descended into this *Kālacakra* for the ultimate benefit of others, may the one of excellent intellect easily traverse this composition—which sets forth the renowned results of astrology—without obstruction; may the Great Beings grant their approval to this work thus composed.

May the discernment of the fearless Hero, which has reached the path within my own heart, dispel the darkness that has arisen; may the merit [thereof] bear fruit as the wealth of a Victor throughout the three worlds.
Thus ends the *Kālacakrāvatāra*.
